query: Research on refractory multicomponent alloys has emphasized exceptional strength at room and elevated temperatures, while mechanical assessment has relied mainly on compression and has included relatively few tensile studies. WFeNiMo fragments released more chemical energy than tungsten-alloy fragments in thin-steel-target penetration tests, and HfZrTiTa0.53 was reported at 786 MPa yield strength, 1314 MPa compressive strength, and 13.5% terminal strain. This evidence establishes strength and energetic promise but leaves limited tensile ductility, load-bearing reliability, and processability unresolved. Subject to preserving strength and impact-triggered energy release, what single testable hypothesis identifies an intervention for HfZrTiTa0.53 that could improve tensile ductility and uniform elongation? Include the intervention, causal mechanism, directional or quantitative outcomes relative to the reported baseline, the applicable temperature, loading mode, and strain-rate limits, prior evidence from the cited studies, and matched compression, tension, and impact tests with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a controlled thermomechanical treatment to refine and partially recrystallize the grain structure of HfZrTiTa0.53 will enhance its tensile ductility and uniform elongation while preserving its high strength and impact-triggered energy release.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy exhibiting coarse microstructure with a yield strength of approximately 786 MPa, compressive strength around 1314 MPa, and a terminal tensile strain (uniform elongation) of 13.5%.
generation.intervention: Implement a processing route that involves controlled cold or warm rolling followed by a tailored annealing treatment to induce grain refinement and partial recrystallization.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted at room temperature under quasi-static tension at a strain rate of ~10^(-3) s^(-1); matched quasi-static compression and impact tests under similar conditions are used to verify preservation of strength and energy release.
generation.structural_mediator: A refined, homogeneous microstructure with reduced grain size and increased grain boundary density.
generation.mechanism: Grain refinement increases the number of grain boundaries which act as obstacles to dislocation motion but also promote more homogeneous distribution of plastic deformation. This facilitates enhanced dislocation activity (and potentially twinning) during tensile loading, thereby delaying the onset of necking and increasing uniform elongation without substantially compromising the alloy’s yield strength or its capacity for impact-triggered energy release.
generation.predicted_outcome: Tensile uniform elongation is expected to increase from the baseline of 13.5% to around 25–30% while maintaining a yield strength near 786 MPa and similar impact energy release characteristics.
generation.baseline: 786 MPa yield strength, 1314 MPa compressive strength, and 13.5% tensile elongation in the as-cast HfZrTiTa0.53 alloy.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is applicable under room temperature quasi-static tensile conditions (strain rate ~10^(-3) s^(-1)). Effects outside these loading conditions or with different processing parameters are uncertain.
generation.uncertainty: The precise processing parameters needed to achieve the targeted microstructure and the exact quantitative improvement in ductility are not yet known; there may be trade-offs with secondary properties that require experimental optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HfZrTiTa0.53 samples: one set in the as-cast (baseline) condition and another set processed via the proposed rolling plus annealing route. Perform standardized tensile tests at room temperature (strain rate ~10^(-3) s^(-1)), along with compression and impact tests to assess energy release.
measurements: Grain size and microstructural homogeneity (via microscopy)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the thermomechanically processed samples do not show a significant increase in tensile uniform elongation (e.g., remain below ~20% or no statistically significant improvement over 13.5%) or if yield strength and/or impact energy release are substantially reduced relative to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Fully recrystallized FG Co33Cr24Ni33V10 alloys, CR750 and CR800, were produced by cold rolling at room temperature and heat treatment. By conducting tensile tests and microstructure characterization, the main conclusions can be summarized as follows: The Co33Cr24Ni33V10 alloy maintained a single-phase FCC structure and exhibited superior phase stability throughout the processes of rolling, heat treatment, and tensile deformation. The primary deformation mechanisms of the CR750 and CR800 alloys were dislocation slip and SFs, with no occurrence of twinning or phase transformation. The fully recrystallized FG structure of CR750 alloy with the minimum mean grain size of 0.95 μm exhibited a high yield strength of 1060 MPa and a uniform elongation of 24.1%. The exceptional strength can be attributed to the presence of the FG structure and solid solution strengthening effect, while the remarkable ductility arises from the excellent strain-hardening ability primarily governed by dislocations and SFs.

Three variants of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) from the AlCoCuFeNi group, containing different amounts of Al and Cu, were developed and produced via induction melting and casting into ceramic moulds. The ingots were homogenized at 1000 °C for 10 h. Analyses revealed that variations in Al and Cu concentrations led to significant changes in the material’s microstructure, hardness, strength, and impact strength. In the equiatomic variant, differential scanning calorimetry revealed a peak associated with the phase transformation, indicating that this alloy’s microstructure consists of two distinct phases. In contrast, when the concentrations of Al and Cu are reduced, a single-phase microstructure is observed. The equiatomic variant (used as a reference) is characterized by its hardness and brittleness, exhibiting slight ductility, with a tensile strength of 80 MPa, a hardness of 400 HV5, and an impact strength of 1.9 J/cm2. However, with adjusted Al contents of 1/2 and Cu contents of 1/4, the alloy displays exceptional strength combined with good plasticity, achieving a tensile strength of up to 450 MPa with 60% elongation, and an impact strength of 215 J/cm2. The eutectic AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy, with an fcc/B2 dual-phase constitution and a uniform and fine lamellar microstructure, exhibited the combination of both high fracture strength and high ductility, which has never been achieved in previously reported HEAs. The room temperature tensile test showed a fracture stress of 944 MPa and an elongation of 25.6%, from the engineering stress-strain curve given in Fig. 4a. These values converted to 1186 MPa and 22.8% in the true stress/strain condition. Noteworthily, this alloy exhibited an ultra-high strain hardening behavior, having the proof stress (the proof stress is determined by shifting the linear elastic curve to 0.2% strain. We choose to not to call it the yield stress, as the mechanism for such a low elastic limit is still unclear at this stage.) of 75 MPa but reaching the fracture stress close to 1.2 GPa. At elevated temperatures of 600 and 700°C (Fig. 4b), the proof stress, fracture stress and elongation were 95 MPa, 806 MPa, 33.7%, and 108 MPa, 538 MPa, 22.9%, respectively, both in the true stress/strain condition.
